meta.title: Who really said "It is better to light a candle than to curse the darkness"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not a JFK original. Quote Investigator traces this proverb to W. L. Watkinson’s 1907 sermon; Kennedy only paraphrased it in 1960.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It is better to light a candle than to curse the darkness'?
meta.ogDescription: Not a JFK original. The line is tentatively traced to W. L. Watkinson’s 1907 sermon and was popularized as the Christophers’ motto.

answer.label: Not John F. Kennedy — a proverb he only paraphrased
answer.authorDates: 1838–1925 · English Wesleyan Methodist minister (earliest documented instance)
answer.sourceLine: John F. Kennedy never used this exact wording. In his July 1960 Democratic nomination acceptance speech he offered a paraphrase — “We are not here to curse the darkness, but to light the candle that can guide us thru that darkness…” — and the saying is widely mislabeled a JFK original. Quote Investigator ↗ tentatively traces the expression to W. L. Watkinson’s 1907 sermon “The Invincible Strategy,” and the modern motto was popularized decades later by the Christophers.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

source.excerpt: Yet is it far better to light the candle than to curse the darkness.
trail: 1907 — earliest instance. Quote Investigator ↗ locates the earliest version in W. L. Watkinson’s sermon: “Yet is it far better to light the candle than to curse the darkness.”
Late 1940s — the motto. Father James Keller’s Christophers adopted the saying as their motto, a periodical of the day even calling it “an old Chinese proverb,” per Quote Investigator ↗.

1960 — JFK’s paraphrase. Kennedy’s acceptance-speech line (“We are not here to curse the darkness, but to light the candle…”) is a paraphrase, not the proverb; Phrases.org.uk ↗ notes several figures, including Kennedy, are merely “associated” with it.
source.excerptNote: W. L. Watkinson’s 1907 phrasing — the earliest documented form. The tidy modern motto (“It is better to light a candle…”) crystallized later through the Christophers, not through Watkinson or Kennedy.
source.rightsNote: The earliest documented instance appears in Watkinson’s 1907 sermon collection — published well before 1931, so that text is in the public domain in the United States. The polished modern motto is a short proverbial slogan with no single identifiable copyright owner.

author.name: William L. Watkinson
author.heading: About William L. Watkinson
author.bio: William Lonsdale Watkinson was an English Wesleyan Methodist minister, editor and prolific author of sermons and devotional essays. His 1907 collection The Supreme Conquest and Other Sermons Preached in America contains the earliest located version of the candle saying — though Watkinson himself presented it as a familiar figure of speech, so even his authorship is only tentative. He is the person Quote Investigator credits with the earliest documented instance, not the coiner of the polished modern motto.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: This feel-good line is a magnet for famous names. The wording is proverbial, and no single celebrated figure coined it — certainly not in the form usually quoted.

items.why: JFK is the most common modern attribution, but he never used this wording. His July 1960 acceptance speech reworked the image — “We are not here to curse the darkness, but to light the candle…” — which is a paraphrase, per Quote Investigator ↗.
The line became attached to Eleanor Roosevelt after her 1962 death, when Adlai Stevenson invoked the candle image in tribute; there is no evidence she originated or said it, per Quote Investigator ↗.
The “Chinese proverb” tag likely spread because the saying was reprinted in the 1907 missionary journal China’s Millions; Quote Investigator ↗ found no compelling evidence of a Chinese origin.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented version is W. L. Watkinson’s in 1907 — and even that is credited only “tentatively,” because he wrote it as an already-familiar figure of speech, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: The saying works because it compresses a whole ethic — constructive action over complaint — into one homely image. That portability is exactly why it drifts onto whichever admired figure a speaker has in mind: a Methodist preacher, a Catholic media priest, a president, a First Lady.

Kennedy’s 1960 reworking and the Christophers’ adoption as a motto did most to fix it in American memory, which is why the two most confident modern attributions — JFK and the “Chinese proverb” — are both downstream of its popularizers rather than its origin.
